Most modern people will cringe when they hear the terms virtue and/or vice. Today, these are loaded terms, packed down and heavily connoting religious observation. I don't want to reduce their religious significance - there's an extent to which understanding these things at the deepest level cannot happen without God. But, the benefits of grasping virtue and vice can be had without any religious character, and it was Aristotle who showed us that the concepts of virtue and vice can be very usefully understood in psychological terms, so that to some extent even those of you who take themselves as atheists can realize their value.

Both virtues and vices are behavioral habits. They're just habits. When we speak of this or that habit as if it was a virtue, or a vice, we are specifying the behavior, along with it's affect for the individual, and the objective effects on both the individual and the society. But at base, we're just pointing to a habit.

Both virtues and vices install themselves in your being in the exact same way, habituation, making them a function of frequency. The more that you instantiate a given behavior, the more 'available' it becomes to the brain. There is a way of looking at human consciousness that says the primary conscious function is really just to say "No." On this view, the ideas that present themselves to you (about what to do at any moment) are not a matter of you consciously scanning alternatives to pick things out. Rather, your brain automatically 'starts' a certain behavior based on the context of any moment. All that consciousness really is, is something like a veto power. You can 'say no' to this or that behavior, and that removes the choice from the pool available, at which point the brain will automatically load the next most available behavior it think to be appropriate for the situation.

Virtues and vices are ways of categorizing the behaviors which are available to you, and habituation is what causes one thing or another to become more available - understood this way, you can see both virtue and vice as things which can become habit by your consistently NOT SAYING NO to them. The mind-brain begins to favor the behaviors that you reject the least often.

But what makes a virtue virtuous and a vice vicious?

We introduce here the notions of goodness and badness, but only in the most common sense. We distinguish between subjective good/bad, and objective good/bad. In the plainest way, virtues create goodness and vice creates badness. Psychologically and behaviorally, a virtue is a habituated behavior that is good for you, unambiguously. A vice is a habit which negatively impacts your life. A great deal of what I believe diminishes the value of these ideas today is that people equate the badness of vice with something arbitrary, that is, not real badness, but badness according to some revealed set of God's rules. Again, while I don't dismiss the fundamentally religious truth of virtue/vice, I don't think that it's necessary to view badness as issuing from God's rule-set; we can understand goodness and badness in terms that are extremely relevant to our experience.

Take masturbation to pornography for instance. Someone might say that the goodness and badness involved with this behavior is strictly subjective, and even lacking definition. After all, the objection could be raised: "The feeling of being aroused, and yet frustrated, is bad for me. It causes displeasure, distraction, and even aggression. Therefore, masturbation is an overall good for me because it prevents those bad things from obtaining in my experience."

The key thing to realize about a vice is that it (a) promotes a short-lived good, in the form of pleasure alone and (b) it tends to negate shared good between the vicious person that they may otherwise have in relationship with others. Contrast this with virtue, which promotes (a) ongoing goodness which (b) spreads out from the individual experiencing the good to encompass (and even promote the formation of) relationships with others. Vice always pulls a person into an isolated world of internal pleasure which is fleeting, whereas the virtues tend to create goodness in a way which opens a person up to the world.

The initial difficulty that presents with virtuous behavior is that the beginning of creating a virtue (habit), is often subjectively bad. Herein lies the critical difference. The badness of creating a virtue only obtains because of its corresponding vice. In the pornography/masturbation example, the only badness resulting from abstaining is the initial adjustment to saying NO to the vice. In my experience, and that of others, it takes approximately 90 days to create a virtue, of whatever category, if this is a virtue which you do not currently possess and instead you currently exalt the corresponding vice. The only badness associated with the virtue of abstaining from pornography is the initial difficulty of saying no to the vice. Once the virtue has been created, there is no badness. On the contrary, once a virtue obtains, it causes ONLY goodness, and moreover, a goodness which opens one up to being in the world, instead of causing you to pursue greater and greater isolation and secrets.

Contrast this with a vice. A vice continues to create badness for a person forever. There is never a point where the badness of a vice ceases to be, or even lessens - quite the contrary, with true vices, the badness associated with them grows and makes one's life more secretive and unstable.

Consider for a moment the good of abstaining from masturbation to porn. The initial 90 days might be a haul. You're very likely to struggle, but it might be considered a very small payment, given a life of exalting its corresponding vice. However, when the virtue has been created, just like the vice, it tends to gain a self-perpetuating momentum in which it becomes easier and easier to express the virtue. That is, the virtue becomes more available to you, and more often becomes the behavior that your mind-brain selects. As you lessen the corresponding vice, the virtue of abstinence will begin to demonstrate itself in many ways: the way in which your creative sexual energies are freed up to allocate to more productive things, the way you are more confident in your interactions with others, more confidence with the opposite sex, far better focus and attention capacity, along with a tendency to spend more time doing other things (often more social or public) that connect you to the world instead of your computer.

A virtue changes in that it expands, it grows, and insodoing it pulls you into the world. A vice contracts and shrinks your world.

In modern times, we began to call a certain kind of man a Renaissance man. In the classic period, this would simply have meant a virtuous man. It's so often that we take the idea of a virtuous man to be something like a square, a card, a nerd. The fact is, the ancients understood that what a body of habits called virtues did for a man was to give him attractive qualities, precisely because it attracted him into the world. Renaissance men are often associated with possessing many skills. If one only considers what virtues do for a man, you realize that by calling a man into the world, they put him in precisely the state of being to learn many skills. When a man is not compelled by vice to sit idly and alone, thinking about himself and simple pleasures, his energies draw him to doing things, to confronting things external to himself, naturally causing him to attract learning, ability, and therefore: confidence. The virtuous man is a moral man, but being virtuous involves more than moral behavior, it is the collective of habits that makes a man a man, which makes him attractive, and compelling, and someone that you want to be around.
